newsitem.title: RWANDA: Zaire, Rwanda move closer to war.
newsitem.headline: Zaire, Rwanda move closer to war.

text.p: Zaire and Rwanda moved closer to war on Wednesday with a second day of cross-border artillery exchanges after fighting in eastern Zaire claimed the life of a Roman Catholic archbishop.

The Vatican said on Wednesday that Archbishop Christophe Munzihirwa was killed in the eastern town of Bukavu in an attack on the city on Tuesday. Church sources in Rome said they believed he had been killed in an ambush.
Rwandan Vice-President and Defence Minister Paul Kagame told a news conference in Rwanda's capital Kigali it would be forced to respond if faced with what he termed Zairean aggression.
"If Zaire brings the war to us we shall fight Zaire. That is not a big problem for me. We are ready to fight even though we seek no war with Zaire," said Kagame, also defence minister.
Asked whether Rwanda was edging closer to war with Zaire, he replied: "Going by the declarations made by Zaire there is every indication that we are going in that direction."

Rwandan Lieutenant-Colonel Firmin Kagame later told reporters in this border town he sent "a good-sized" force of troops into Zaire after nightfall on Tuesday in retaliation for Zairean firing into Rwanda.
"After they hit our territory and injured and killed our people and hit civilians we were forced to retaliate," he said.
He said mortar fire hit Cyangugu army barracks on Tuesday. Rwanda's vice-president spoke of several dead in the town.
Zaire, a giant country at the heart of Africa, has long been in chaos but this crisis in its east is seen as potentially the most far-reaching in its 36-year history.
President Mobutu Sese Seko, whose strongarm tactics helped keep his country together, is sick in Switzerland, recovering from cancer surgery. He has not been in Zaire for months.

At the Kagame news conference, Rwandan officials handed out a pamphlet from the president's office calling for a Berlin Two conference of former colonial powers in the region -- France, Germany and Belgium -- to take a renewed look at territorial boundaries and the question of the ethnic Tutsi Banyamulenge.
At a Berlin conference from 1884 to 1885 Belgium set up the Congo Free State, later to become Zaire, under King Leopold.
Deadly rivalry between Hutus and Tutsis, which resulted in nearly one million dead in the 1994 genocide in Rwanda, has spilled into Zaire, host to 1.1 million Hutu Rwandan refugees.
The International Committee of the Red Cross said volunteers in the town of Bukavu were burying bodies after fighting between Tutsi rebels and troops to lessen the threat of disease.
The last foreign aid workers fled from Bukavu on Tuesday.
"The missionaries said it was impossible to go out because of the possibility of being shot and they were staying in their house," a Burundian priest said.
A Roman Catholic priest in Bukavu said on Wednesday the town was completely cut off from aid supplies and thousands of refugees in the region were in danger of starving to death.
"We are beginning to run short of food. At this rate, we are all going to die of hunger," Abbe Pierre Cibambo said in a statement issued by the charity CAFOD.
He said order had broken down, preventing any aid work.
In diplomatic moves, the United Nations in New York said Canada's ambassador to Washington, Raymond Chretien, was appointed as a special envoy to help resolve the crisis.
French President Jacques Chirac on Wednesday urged heads of east and central African states to call a conference quickly on the rapidly deteriorating situation on the Zaire-Rwanda border.
The European Union wants the Organisation of African Unity to send troops to guarantee the safety of the refugees in Zaire, an Irish government minister said on Wednesday.
"There should be a force to monitor and protect refugees. This should be from the OAU with logistical support from the EU," said Joan Burton, minister of state for overseas aid.
Fighting inside Zaire pits Zairean army troops against Tutsi rebels apparently receiving support from Tutsi-led Rwanda.
The Rwandan refugees in Zaire are Hutus who perpetrated the 1994 genocide of Tutsis and do not want to return to Rwanda, fearing death or jail if they return.
About half a million of the refugees in Zaire are now out of contact with U.N. agencies because of the fighting.

On Wednesday a Reuters reporter at the Rwandan town of Gisenyi said he could hear heavy firing near the town of Goma. He estimated that fighting between Zairean troops and rebels had reached within 10 km (six miles) of Goma city.
He also reported fighting four km (two miles) from Kibumba refugee camp, which was emptied on Saturday and is north of Goma, with anti-aircraft batteries, mortars and machineguns.
An aid official in the city said planeloads of Zairean troop reinforcements landed at Goma airport on Wednesday.

Aid workers in Goma said Rumamgabo village, also a Zairean military base 35 km (20 miles) north of Goma city, was hit with mortars on Wednesday and fighting seemed to be moving towards Katale and Kahindo camps housing more than 300,000 refugees.
Even refugees still in camps are receiving minimal food aid because the U.N. is afraid that supplies will soon run out.
The U.N. is trying to avoid a repeat of 1994, when thousands died daily of cholera and dysentery in eastern Zaire camps.
